claim: Social behavior in mammals is often studied in pairs under artificial conditions.
source_text: Social behavior in mammals is often studied in pairs under artificial conditions, yet groups may rely on more complicated social structures.
evidence_reasoning: This is a statement about common practice in the field, reflecting established knowledge about how social behavior research is typically conducted.

claim: Minimal models that rely only on individual traits and pairwise correlations between animals are not enough to capture group behavior in mice.
source_text: We have found that the minimal models that rely only on individual traits and pairwise correlations between animals are not enough to capture group behavior, but that models that include third-order interactions give a very accurate description of the group.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by experimental data from tracking mice and mathematical modeling showing that pairwise models explain only ~60% of group correlations, requiring inference from the modeling results.

claim: Models that include third-order interactions give a very accurate description of mouse group behavior.
source_text: We have found that the minimal models that rely only on individual traits and pairwise correlations between animals are not enough to capture group behavior, but that models that include third-order interactions give a very accurate description of the group.
evidence_reasoning: Supported by data showing third-order models capture ~90% of group correlations, with inference from maximum entropy modeling framework.

claim: Environmental complexity during adolescence affects the collective group behavior of adult mice.
source_text: Using this approach, we show that environmental complexity during adolescence affects the collective group behavior of adult mice, in particular altering the role of high-order structure.
evidence_reasoning: This is directly supported by experimental data comparing standard environment (SE) and complex environment (CE) groups showing different correlation structures.

claim: Environmental complexity during adolescence alters the role of high-order structure in adult mouse group behavior.
source_text: Using this approach, we show that environmental complexity during adolescence affects the collective group behavior of adult mice, in particular altering the role of high-order structure.
evidence_reasoning: Supported by data showing CE groups had higher pairwise contribution (74.6% vs 61.9%) and lower fourth-order contribution compared to SE groups.

claim: Coherence of collective behavior patterns in large groups of animals presents fundamental questions relating to distributed information processing, computation, and learning.
source_text: The coherence of 'collective behavior' patterns of large groups of animals, such as insect swarms (Buhl et al., 2006; Simpson et al., 2006) fish schools (Sumpter et al., 2008; Katz et al., 2011), bird flocks (Cavagna et al., 2010; Nagy et al., 2010), and human crowds (Song et al., 2010; Gallup et al., 2012), presents us with fundamental questions relating to distributed information processing, computation, and learning.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work and reflects established knowledge in the field about collective behavior.

claim: Individual traits may play an important role in shaping group behavior in smaller groups of animals.
source_text: Smaller groups of animals present an interesting and sometimes more difficult scenario, where individual traits may play an important role in shaping the group behavior (Lathe, 2004).
evidence_reasoning: Supported by citation to prior work and reflects established understanding about small group dynamics.

claim: Much of our understanding of social behavior has come from studies of just pairs of animals under artificial settings.
source_text: Yet, much of our understanding of social behavior has come from studies of just pairs of animals under artificial settings (Insel and Fernald, 2004; Langford et al., 2006; Moy et al., 2008; Branson et al., 2009; Dankert et al., 2009; Blumstein et al., 2010; Silverman et al., 2010; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011; de Chaumont et al., 2012).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: It is not clear what the detailed analysis of social interaction at the level of a single pair implies for larger groups.
source_text: It is not clear, however, what the detailed analysis of social interaction at the level of a single pair implies for larger groups.
evidence_reasoning: This reflects a gap in current knowledge and sets up the motivation for the study.

claim: New features may emerge that characterize the group as a whole that cannot be inferred from the study of individuals or pairs.
source_text: In particular, new features may emerge that characterize the group as a whole that cannot be inferred from the study of individuals or pairs (Cavagna et al., 2010).
evidence_reasoning: Supported by citation and reflects theoretical understanding of emergent group properties.

claim: Individual mice in the group had distinct personal preferences for certain locations.
source_text: We found that individual mice in the group had distinct personal preferences for certain locations (Figure 1E), and the relative amounts of time spent in different places.
evidence_reasoning: Directly supported by observational data shown in Figure 1E from tracking experiments.

claim: The amount of time that each mouse spent continuously at each location had a power-law-like behavior.
source_text: Despite these individual differences, the amount of time that each mouse spent continuously at each location had a power-law-like behavior (Figure 1F).
evidence_reasoning: Supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1F demonstrating power-law distribution.

claim: The power-law distribution of time spent at locations was similar for different mice when analyzed individually.
source_text: This power-law distribution was similar for the different mice, when they were each analyzed individually, despite their individual differences on other parameters.
evidence_reasoning: Supported by comparative analysis of individual mouse behavior patterns.

claim: Knowing the location of one mouse gives relatively little information about the location of another (typically less than 5%).
source_text: We found that knowing the location of one mouse gives relatively little information about that of another—typically less than 5% (averaged on all pairs, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence_reasoning: Directly supported by mutual information calculations from experimental data.

claim: Knowing the joint locations of three mice gives much more information about the fourth one (on average 25% of location entropy).
source_text: However, knowing the joint locations of three mice gives much more information about that of the fourth one—over all groups and mice I(xi;{xj,xk,xl}) was, on average, 25% of H(xi).
evidence_reasoning: Supported by information-theoretic calculations from tracking data.

claim: The information about the location of one mouse from the locations of the other mice is highly synergistic.
source_text: Figure 2C shows that this information was highly synergistic—namely that the information about the location of one mouse that can be read from the locations of the other mice can be more than double the sum of pairwise information values of that mouse with all the others
evidence_reasoning: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C comparing joint information to sum of pairwise information.

claim: The group is much more complex than even the full collection of pairs.
source_text: Thus, the group is not only more complex than a collection of individuals, but much more complex than even the full collection of pairs.
evidence_reasoning: Inferred from the synergistic information results showing group complexity exceeds pairwise predictions.

claim: The remaining 75% of uncertainty about the location of each mouse is the level of individuality that cannot be explained by the location of other mice.
source_text: The remaining 75% of uncertainty about the location of each mouse is exactly the level of individuality of each mouse, which cannot be explained in terms of the location of the other mice.
evidence_reasoning: Calculated from information-theoretic analysis showing 25% predictability leaves 75% individual variation.

claim: Maximum entropy models provide the most parsimonious explanation that does not make additional assumptions beyond required features.
source_text: Since the entropy of a distribution measures its randomness of lack of structure, then among all models that are consistent with some desired feature of the data, the maximum entropy model is the most parsimonious explanation that does not make any additional assumptions beyond the required features.
evidence_reasoning: This is a statement about the mathematical properties of maximum entropy models, reflecting established theory.

claim: The minimal maximum entropy model is mathematically unique and can be found numerically.
source_text: This minimal model is mathematically unique and can be found numerically (Schneidman et al., 2003).
evidence_reasoning: Supported by citation to prior methodological work establishing the mathematical properties.

claim: Maximum entropy models have been successfully used to infer functional dependencies between neurons, genes, proteins and more.
source_text: Such models have been successfully used to infer functional dependencies between neurons, genes, proteins and more (e.g., Schneidman et al., 2006; Ganmor et al., 2011; Lezon et al., 2007; Marre et al., 2009; Mora et al., 2010; Stephens et al., 2010; Stephens et al., 2013; Bialek et al., 2012).
evidence_reasoning: Supported by multiple citations to prior applications of the method.

claim: The independent model (first-order model) is insufficient to describe the behavior of the group.
source_text: As it was clear already from Figure 2B, the independent model is insufficient to describe the behavior of the group.
evidence_reasoning: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B comparing independent model predictions to observed distributions.

claim: The contribution of the pairwise ME model was 57.2% ± 10.2% of total group correlations.
source_text: We found that over all groups, the contribution of the pairwise ME model, given by I(2) was 57.2% ± 10.2% of IN.
evidence_reasoning: Directly reported quantitative result from analysis of all experimental groups.

claim: Third-order interactions carry nearly a third of the total correlations.
source_text: We found that I(3) carried nearly a third of the total correlations, and so p(3) that relies on individual traits, pairwise and triple interactions between the mice explains 92.8% ± 2.9% of the correlations
evidence_reasoning: Quantitative result from maximum entropy model analysis of experimental data.

claim: For a group of four mice, even using all pairwise interactions is not enough to capture the group behavior.
source_text: Thus, for a group of four mice even using all pairwise interactions is not enough to capture the group behavior; the third-order interactions are therefore necessary and capture about a third of the correlation structure.
evidence_reasoning: Inferred from the quantitative results showing pairwise models explain only ~60% of correlations.

claim: The third-order interactions are necessary to capture group behavior and capture about a third of the correlation structure.
source_text: Thus, for a group of four mice even using all pairwise interactions is not enough to capture the group behavior; the third-order interactions are therefore necessary and capture about a third of the correlation structure.
evidence_reasoning: Directly supported by the I(3) contribution measurements from the data.

claim: The strong high-order dependency is consistent with the synergistic effect in information about mouse location from other mice.
source_text: This strong high-order dependency is consistent with the synergistic effect seen in Figure 2 in terms of the information that can be read about the location of a mouse from that of the other mice.
evidence_reasoning: Inference connecting two different analyses (synergistic information and high-order model contributions) of the same data.

claim: The parameters of maximum entropy models can be interpreted as functional social interactions between animals.
source_text: The parameters of the maximum entropy models can be interpreted as functional social interactions between the animals (similar to the parameters of the corresponding Potts models from physics).
evidence_reasoning: This interpretation is based on analogy to physics models and theoretical understanding of the model parameters.

claim: Functional interactions reflect statistical dependencies and will probably differ from explicit physical interactions between animals.
source_text: We emphasize that these functional interactions reflect statistical dependencies, and will probably differ from explicit physical interactions between the animals that one could measure.
evidence_reasoning: This is a cautionary statement about interpretation, involving speculation about the relationship between statistical and physical interactions.

claim: Statistical dependencies highlight the most prominent relations that underlie patterns of group behavior.
source_text: Yet, these statistical dependencies highlight the most prominent relations that underlie the patterns of group behavior.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference about what the statistical analysis reveals about group behavior.

claim: The strongest functional interactions correspond to events that are most surprising or not predicted from lower orders of interactions.
source_text: The strongest functional interactions corresponded not to the most frequent events, but rather to those events that are most surprising or not predicted from lower orders of interactions, thus presenting interactions of a truly social nature.
evidence_reasoning: Inferred from analysis of the interaction parameters in relation to event frequencies.

claim: The dominant interactions in the group are negative ones (compound configurations that tend not to happen).
source_text: Our results show that the dominant interactions in the group are negative ones, namely compound configurations that tend not to happen compared to expectations based on individual behavior.
evidence_reasoning: Supported by analysis of interaction parameters shown in Figure 4.

claim: Negative interactions may suggest competition as a dominant force in the social structure.
source_text: This may suggest competition as a dominant force in the social structure.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative interpretation of the negative interaction findings.

claim: The relative sparseness of interaction maps indicates that a small number of social events can have a strong, macroscopic impact on the group.
source_text: In addition, the relative sparseness of the interaction maps indicates that even a small number of social events can have a strong, macroscopic impact on the group.
evidence_reasoning: Inferred from the sparse structure of the regularized interaction maps.

claim: Growing up in a complex environment resulted in groups that were far less correlated as a group.
source_text: We found that growing up in a complex environment with more mice, which better resembles a natural habitat, resulted in groups that were far less correlated as a group, and their social structure could be explained to a much larger degree based on pairwise interactions.
evidence_reasoning: Supported by comparison of correlation measures between SE and CE groups.

claim: Complex environment groups' social structure could be explained to a much larger degree based on pairwise interactions.
source_text: We found that growing up in a complex environment with more mice, which better resembles a natural habitat, resulted in groups that were far less correlated as a group, and their social structure could be explained to a much larger degree based on pairwise interactions.
evidence_reasoning: Supported by data showing CE groups had 74.6% pairwise contribution vs 61.9% for SE groups.

claim: The total group correlation values of SE and CE groups were similar on the first day.
source_text: We found that the total group correlation IN values of the SE and CE groups were similar on the first day, but then the SE groups became more correlated.
evidence_reasoning: Directly supported by multi-information measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: SE groups became more correlated over time while CE groups' correlations remained unchanged.
source_text: We found that the total group correlation IN values of the SE and CE groups were similar on the first day, but then the SE groups became more correlated. In contrast, the correlations among the CE mice remained unchanged (Figure 5D).
evidence_reasoning: Supported by temporal analysis of multi-information across 4 days shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There was a progressive increase in social correlation ('socialization') in SE groups that was absent in CE groups.
source_text: In other words, there was a progressive increase in social correlation, or 'socialization' in the SE groups, which was absent in the CE groups.
evidence_reasoning: Inferred from the temporal patterns of correlation changes between SE and CE groups.

claim: The contribution of pairwise interaction to full group correlations was higher in CE groups than SE groups (74.6% ± 2.5% vs 61.9% ± 2.4%).
source_text: In the CE groups the contribution of pairwise interaction to the full group correlations was higher than in SE groups (74.6% ± 2.5% in CE groups compared to 61.9% ± 2.4% for the SE ones, averaged over all four days).
evidence_reasoning: Quantitative result from analysis of interaction order contributions across experimental groups.

claim: CE groups showed virtually no contribution of fourth-order interactions.
source_text: The dominance of the low-order interactions was also reflected by the virtual lack of contribution of fourth-order interaction in the CE groups, whereas the SE groups showed more complex high-order structure
evidence_reasoning: Supported by analysis of fourth-order contributions shown in Figure 5E.

claim: SE groups showed more complex high-order structure with fourth-order interactions contributing 6.0% ± 0.7% to total correlation.
source_text: The dominance of the low-order interactions was also reflected by the virtual lack of contribution of fourth-order interaction in the CE groups, whereas the SE groups showed more complex high-order structure (fourth-order interactions contribution to the total correlation in the SE groups was 6.0% ± 0.7% [Figure 5E]).
evidence_reasoning: Quantitative result from fourth-order model analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In CE groups, information from three mice about the fourth was far less synergistic than in SE groups.
source_text: In the CE groups the information from three mice about the fourth was far less synergistic than in the case of SE groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence_reasoning: Supported by information-theoretic analysis comparing SE and CE groups.

claim: Mice exposed to complex environment during adolescence were more individual.
source_text: Thus, mice exposed to a complex environment during adolescence were more individual, and their weaker group correlations relied more on pairwise rather than higher-order dependencies.
evidence_reasoning: Inferred from the combination of lower correlations and higher pairwise contributions in CE groups.

claim: CE mice's weaker group correlations relied more on pairwise rather than higher-order dependencies.
source_text: Thus, mice exposed to a complex environment during adolescence were more individual, and their weaker group correlations relied more on pairwise rather than higher-order dependencies.
evidence_reasoning: Directly supported by the breakdown of correlation contributions by order.

claim: Quantifying social interactions presents an ethological challenge both experimentally and theoretically.
source_text: Quantifying social interactions presents an ethological challenge both experimentally and theoretically (Adolphs, 2010).
evidence_reasoning: Statement about the state of the field supported by citation.

claim: Species that live in groups display profoundly more complex social repertoires than solitary species.
source_text: While even solitary species display social behavior such as mating, aggression, and maternal care, species that live in groups display profoundly more complex social repertoires (Silk, 2013).
evidence_reasoning: Statement about animal behavior supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Group behavior is likely to depend on environmental context.
source_text: This group behavior, ideally dissected into individual and group parts, is also likely to depend on the environmental context (Insel and Fernald, 2004).
evidence_reasoning: Statement about behavioral ecology supported by citation.

claim: Mice are an ideal model organism for investigating social behavior in mammals and the neural mechanisms that underlie it.
source_text: Mice are an ideal model organism for investigating social behavior in mammals and the neural mechanisms that underlie it.
evidence_reasoning: Statement about the utility of mice as a model system, reflecting established practice in the field.

claim: Mice live in groups and form diverse societies with different characteristics such as group size, hierarchy, aggression, and social tolerance.
source_text: Together with the ability to manipulate their genomic make-up (Lewandoski, 2001), and record neural activity (electrophysiologically or optically), mice live in groups and form diverse societies with different characteristics such as group size, hierarchy, aggression, and social tolerance (Bronson, 1979).
evidence_reasoning: Statement about mouse social behavior supported by citation.

claim: Current methodologies for analysis of social behavior in mice have focused mainly on dyadic interactions.
source_text: However, despite the complex nature of their social organization, the current methodologies used for analysis of social behavior in mice have focused mainly on dyadic interactions such as in the classical three-chamber social approach test and the partition test (Silverman et al., 2010).
evidence_reasoning: Statement about current methods in the field supported by citation.

claim: The tracking system enables automatic tracking of group behavior of mice in the dark over long periods of time in a semi-natural environment with high spatiotemporal resolution while maintaining individual identities.
source_text: The system we introduce here enables automatic tracking of group behavior of mice in the dark, over long periods of time, and in a semi-natural environment, with high spatiotemporal resolution while maintaining individual identities.
evidence_reasoning: Description of the experimental system's capabilities, supported by the methods and results presented.

claim: RFID-based systems allow for tracking of a very large number of animals.
source_text: We note that RFID-based systems allow for the tracking of a very large number of animals, whereas our tracking capacity depends on the number of distinguishable dyes and spatial marking patterns on the mice
evidence_reasoning: Statement about capabilities of RFID systems, reflecting established knowledge about the technology.

claim: The strength of the color-based tracking system is in its much higher spatial and temporal resolution compared to RFID systems.
source_text: However, the strength of our system is in its much higher spatial and temporal resolution, and the ability to track and analyze details of individual behavior of the animals and between them.
evidence_reasoning: Comparative statement about system capabilities based on technical understanding.

claim: The pairwise-based model of the group could only explain approximately 60% of the correlation structure.
source_text: Intriguingly, the pairwise-based model of the group that assumed no higher-order contribution could only explain approximately 60% of the correlation structure in the group
evidence_reasoning: Quantitative result from maximum entropy model analysis.

claim: Models that included third-order dependencies captured approximately 90% of the group correlation structure.
source_text: whereas models that included also third-order dependencies (but not fourth-order ones) captured approximately 90% of the group correlation structure.
evidence_reasoning: Quantitative result from third-order maximum entropy model analysis.

claim: Three-quarters of the uncertainty about the location of a mouse comes from its own individuality.
source_text: That is, the mice still have a significant individual component, even given the other mice.
evidence_reasoning: Inferred from the 25% predictability leaving 75% individual variation.

claim: Most social behaviors such as fights, chases, courtship, and grooming are usually observed in pairs.
source_text: The need for models that include high-order interactions is surprising, since intuitively one might have expected that it would be possible to construct a mathematically accurate description of the group once all the interactions between pairs of mice were known. After all, most social behaviors, such as fights, chases, courtship, and grooming, are usually observed in pairs.
evidence_reasoning: Statement about typical social behaviors reflecting established ethological knowledge.

claim: In almost all prior applications of maximum entropy models to biological networks, the contribution of pairwise interactions was very large and dominated the network structure.
source_text: Interestingly, in almost all these cases the contribution of pairwise interactions was very large and dominated the network structure, especially in small networks—in clear contrast to what we found for the mice.
evidence_reasoning: Statement about prior findings in the literature, contrasting with current results.

claim: The dominant interactions in the group are negative ones, which may suggest competition as a dominant force.
source_text: Our results show that the dominant interactions in the group are negative ones, namely compound configurations that tend not to happen compared to expectations based on individual behavior. This may suggest competition as a dominant force in the social structure.
evidence_reasoning: Data shows negative interactions dominate; competition interpretation is speculative.

claim: The tracking algorithm achieved 99.6% accuracy compared to human labeling.
source_text: Validation of the tracking algorithm was performed by comparing the algorithm's performance to human labeling of 500 randomly chosen frames, which gave 99.6% accuracy.
evidence_reasoning: Quantitative validation result from comparison to ground truth.

claim: The arena consisted of a 70 cm × 50 cm × 50 cm cage with several objects including a Z-shaped wall, water dispenser, two feeders, nests, an elevated block, and ramps.
source_text: The arena consisted of a 70 cm × 50 cm × 50 cm cage that included several objects: a Z-shaped wall, a water dispenser, two feeders, a small nest and a large nest, an elevated block, and two elevated ramps.
evidence_reasoning: Direct description of the experimental apparatus used in the study.

claim: Mice spent much more time in certain locations in the arena.
source_text: Mice spent much more time in certain locations in the arena (see 'heat map' in Figure 1D).
evidence_reasoning: Observational result from tracking data shown in heat map.

claim: The behavior of 17 groups of mice was analyzed, each composed of four adult mice.
source_text: We analyzed the behavior of 17 groups of mice, each composed of four adult mice in an arena resembling an ethologically relevant context that has an interesting environment for exploration
evidence_reasoning: Description of the experimental sample and design.

claim: The maximum entropy models are a generalized form of the Potts model from statistical physics.
source_text: The maximum entropy models we have used to describe the group behavior are a generalized form of the Potts model from statistical physics, which describes the behavior of spins in a lattice in terms of the interactions between them
evidence_reasoning: Statement about the mathematical relationship between models, based on established theory.
